rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## Why the course opens here Every other unit will hand you something to judge — a family argument, an advert, a politician's promise — and this unit is where you get the tools to judge it. Critical thinking sounds like a laboratory word, but it is really just reading with your guard up: enjoying the writer's music while checking whether the words can actually carry the weight they claim.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Question assumptions before accepting claims — apply this to the unit's own readings.
Distinguish fact, opinion and belief in any passage; examiners test this directly.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ## The grammar and style of thinking clearly Clear thought has a sound, and English gives it a grammar. Strong arguments move through **connectives** the way traffic moves through lights: *because* and *since* open the reasons; *therefore, thus, consequently* deliver the verdict; *however, although, admittedly* let the other side onto the road — safely.…  ·  ## Speaking and writing the theme — a model, dissected Here is a paragraph in the shape examiners reward, annotated as a teacher would mark it. *"Social media should be taught, not banned. **(claim, stated once and plainly)** Admittedly, the harm is real — a phone feeds on the very hours homework needs.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## How the exam asks it The paper returns to the same four moves. **"Identify the writer's claim/assumption"** — quote or paraphrase the claim, then supply the hidden floor: "The argument assumes that…". **"Fact or opinion?"** — label, then justify in one clause ("opinion — it says *should*, and no one can check a *should*").…  ·  **Critical thinking toolkit (classified)** | Skill | Question it asks | Exam use | |---|---|---| | Claim spotting | What is being asserted? | 2-m identify claim | | Evidence check | What backs it? | 4-m assess support | | Assumption hunt | What is taken for granted? | 4-m expose premise | | Counter-view | What would a critic say? | 8-m balanced answer | | Verdict | Where does the weight lie? | 8-m conclusion |

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. What assumption does the writer's argument rest on? (2 marks) — identify the unstated premise and explain how the claim depends on it.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The words that carry the theme English keeps its sharpest thinking-words in everyday clothes, and the examiners know it. A **fact** can be checked — "Nepal joined the UN in 1955" either stands or falls. An **opinion** can only be argued — "Momo is better than pizza" will outlive us all unresolved. A **belief** is held on trust — "good things happen to good people" — precious, perhaps, but never proof.…  ·  ## Reading like a detective — the devices of persuasion Writers who want your agreement rarely argue honestly, and English has names for their favourite tricks. Learn the names and the tricks lose their power. **Loaded language** smuggles the conclusion into the description: a "regime" and a "government" may govern identically, but one has already been condemned.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Unit questions test argument evaluation — find the writer's CLAIM, the EVIDENCE and the ASSUMPTION; a missing-evidence comment earns the analysis mark.  ·  Trick 2: For 'do you agree?' items, use the 3-step reply: concede one point, refute with evidence, restate your position.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. Give one counter-argument to the writer's claim. (2 marks) — state it fairly, then say why it is weaker.
